By owning a majority of the vault shares during the interest payment, they effectively receive most of their own interest back, resulting in nearly interest-free loans. This creates a significant financial vulnerability in the system.

• initialize() is public and has no access control – the first account that calls it becomes the vault’s admin/manager addresses set in the nested __WasabiVault_init().
• If the proxy/implementation is ever deployed without an immediate initialisation-tx, anyone can seize control (“uninitialised-upgradeable-contract” vulnerability).
• External call token.claim() is executed before the critical state variable totalAssetValue is updated.
• A malicious rebasing token could call back into the vault (deposit / withdraw / flash-loan, etc.) while the state is still outdated, breaking accounting or stealing funds.
• Any user can mint / burn 1 wei of shares between the admin’s off-chain reading of totalSupply and the on-chain transaction, permanently blocking yield claims (grief / denial-of-service).
• claimGas(contractAddress, recipient) lets the admin pass any contractAddress.
• If the underlying Blast implementation does not check that msg.sender == contractAddress, the admin can siphon gas rebates belonging to other contracts.

• token.claim() and future ERC-20 transfers are called directly.  Non-standard tokens that do not return a boolean (or that revert on failure) can lock the vault or make it believe a transfer succeeded when it didn’t.
• Both claimGas() and claimYield() are onlyAdmin.  A compromised admin key can steal all gas, block yield, or brick the vault.  No multisig / timelock mitigation is enforced in this layer.
• The vault assumes WETH or USDB are the only yield-bearing assets.  If Blast later introduces new rebasing tokens, the function will revert and prevent yield claims until the contract is upgraded.
8. Lack of events for critical actions
• claimGas() performs value-transfers but emits no event, reducing auditability and off-chain monitoring.
